planting.note: Plant container-grown seedlings in spring in deep, lean, extremely fast-draining soil in full sun; quiver tree needs decades of frost-free growth to reach its tree form, so treat it as a long-term specimen or large container plant outside of zone 9-11.

directions: Unlike the branching, shrubby torch aloe or the spreading colonies of soap aloe, quiver tree grows as a single, slow-thickening trunk that can eventually tower 20-30 feet tall in its native Namibian and South African desert habitat, topped by a dense crown of blue-gray rosettes. Its smooth, golden-brown, papery bark peels in flakes and was historically hollowed out by San hunters to make quivers for arrows, giving the species its common name. Branching begins only after many years, when the crown forks repeatedly to form a rounded, candelabra-like canopy quite different from the single unbranched rosette of most tree-form aloes. Grow in full sun with maximum drainage and expect glacially slow growth for the first decade; mature specimens are extremely long-lived and drought tolerant, producing bright yellow flower spikes in winter that are a critical nectar source for sunbirds and bees in the Namib and Succulent Karoo.

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in lean, sharply draining soil in full sun; Aden aloe develops its richest purple-red winter color under bright light and minimal water.

directions: Native to the mountains of Yemen and adjacent Saudi Arabia, Aden aloe forms wide, arching rosettes of blue-green leaves edged in small hooked orange teeth that bleed a fluorescent green sap drying to dark violet, a trait not shared with the South African species already in this collection. Foliage flushes purple in full sun and deepens to an intense violet-red through winter cold, giving the plant its epithet 'rubroviolacea' and making it one of the most dramatically colored landscape aloes when stressed. As the thick stem elongates with age it tends to sprawl and lean rather than stay upright, eventually forming a loose clump as basal offsets appear. Established plants send up unbranched spires of dense red flowers up to 30 inches tall each winter, a bolder and more concentrated bloom than the branched spikes of many other South African aloes.
sources: Kew Science - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Grow in a shallow dish or small pot of very fast-draining, mineral succulent mix in bright, filtered light; this is the smallest cultivated aloe species and rots quickly if watered like a full-size aloe.

directions: Aloe descoingsii is the smallest known species in the genus, forming individual rosettes barely 1.5 inches across, dwarfed by every other aloe in this collection including the compact hybrids Blue Elf and Christmas Carol. Critically endangered in its native southern Madagascar, it offsets extremely freely, eventually filling a shallow dish or pot with dozens to hundreds of tiny, dull-green, white-warted rosettes rather than growing into a single larger plant. Slender flower stalks only a few inches tall carry small scarlet, orange-tipped urn-shaped flowers in spring and summer, tiny even by miniature-aloe standards. Because of its minute size it needs lighter shade and far less water than typical landscape aloes, and is almost always grown as a collector's houseplant rather than outdoors.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; bottlebrush aloe is among the least cold-hardy of the tree aloes and needs a frost-free site or large container.

directions: Bottlebrush aloe grows as a fast single, unbranched trunk with leaves held in tight, overlapping spiraling ranks rather than the loose, open rosette of mountain aloe or the branching candelabra form of torch aloe. Its dense, cylindrical flower spikes, packed with coral to salmon-pink tubular flowers along the entire length of an unbranched stalk, resemble a bottle-cleaning brush and give the species its common name, in contrast to the branched flower heads typical of most South African tree aloes. It is one of the fastest-growing tree aloes in cultivation, capable of reaching significant height within a decade in a frost-free subtropical climate, but is markedly more cold-sensitive than mountain aloe or Cape aloe and needs full frost protection. Native to humid, subtropical grasslands and forest margins of eastern South Africa and Eswatini, it tolerates more humidity than most aloes without leaf rot.

planting.note: Plant nursery starts in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; book aloe holds its distinctive two-fan juvenile shape for years before shifting to a rosette, so avoid disturbing young plants unnecessarily.

directions: Book aloe is named for its unusual juvenile growth habit: leaves stack directly opposite each other in two flat, overlapping ranks like the pages of a book, rather than spiraling into a rosette from the start as in nearly every other aloe in cultivation, including the similarly fan-shaped but tree-forming fan aloe. This distichous phase can persist for years and the plant frequently flowers while still in this two-ranked form, an unusual trait within the genus, before the leaves eventually rearrange into a more conventional rosette with age. Milky blue-gray leaves brighten to a chalky blue-white in strong sun and carry small forked marginal teeth, and brilliant pink flowers in conical spikes appear in winter. Native to grassland habitats in South Africa, Eswatini, and Mozambique, it tolerates colder winters than most Madagascan or tropical aloe species, surviving brief dips into the low twenties Fahrenheit.

planting.note: Grow in a shallow pot of fast-draining, gritty succulent mix in bright light; this species offsets into a dense mound and is easiest to manage in a container rather than the open ground.

directions: As its name suggests, this small Madagascan species looks more like a Haworthia than a typical Aloe, with dark green, fleshy leaves densely covered in soft, white, bristly spines rather than the firm marginal teeth found on most South African aloe species in this collection. It grows tucked into rock crevices in Madagascar's Central Highlands and offsets prolifically from the base, quickly forming a dense mounded clump of small rosettes rather than a single larger plant. Slender flower stalks bear small tubular red to orange flowers in a modest seasonal display, secondary to the plant's appeal as a textural foliage specimen. It is more tolerant of light shade than most true aloes, making it a good candidate for a bright windowsill rather than only full outdoor sun.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring on a well-drained slope in full sun; this Madagascar highland variety tolerates more cold than most of its lowland relatives if grown on a site where cold air drains away.

directions: Unlike most Madagascan aloe species, which tend to be frost-tender lowland plants, this variety of Aloe capitata comes from quartzite outcrops in the island's central highlands above 5,000 feet elevation and has survived brief drops to 20 degrees Fahrenheit in mild California gardens, making it noticeably hardier than typical Madagascan aloes. A single, stemless rosette of milky blue-gray leaves that flush purple under strong sun forms the plant's main feature, staying solitary rather than clustering into offsets the way many smaller aloes do. In late winter its branched flower stalk rises roughly three feet, each branch topped by a rounded cluster of glossy orange buds that open to pale yellow, bell-shaped flowers, a two-tone bud-to-bloom color change distinct from the uniform coral or red flowers of most South African species here. Give it excellent drainage and a site where cold air does not pool to get the best results from its unusual highland cold tolerance.
sources: Kew Science - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Grow in a shallow pot or rock garden pocket of very fast-draining, gritty soil in full sun; this Karoo native is naturally solitary and slow to offset, so avoid dividing it more often than necessary.

directions: This dwarf species from the arid Succulent Karoo of South Africa's Northern Cape forms a small, solitary rosette of smooth, spineless, turquoise-blue leaves without the spots, teeth, or warts found on most other small aloes in this collection, such as hedgehog aloe or tiger tooth aloe. It typically stays single rather than clustering, unlike freely offsetting compact aloes like Crosby's Prolific, though older plants occasionally form a small clump. Flower stalks are disproportionately tall and showy relative to the plant's tiny size, carrying red to orange tubular flowers well above the low foliage in late winter and spring. Native to a genuinely arid climate, it demands extremely sharp drainage and minimal summer water, rotting quickly if kept as moist as larger, more forgiving aloe species.

planting.note: Grow in a shallow pot of fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to light shade; Baker's aloe clusters readily and is best divided every couple of years to keep the mound from crowding itself.

directions: Native to low-elevation rocky hills in southeastern Madagascar, Baker's aloe forms dense clumps of slender, fleshy, reddish-brown leaves heavily mottled with white spots, a mottled coloring closer to soap aloe than to the plain green or blue-gray foliage of most compact aloes covered here. It stays low and wide rather than tall, spreading outward through vigorous clustering that eventually fills a container or garden pocket with a low mound of rosettes rather than growing upward. Tubular red to orange summer flowers appear on multiple stalks through the clump and are attractive to birds and pollinators during the warmer months rather than the winter bloom typical of many South African aloe species. Give it full sun to light shade and good drainage, and divide congested clumps periodically since it offsets more vigorously than most Madagascan dwarf aloes.

planting.note: Plant container-grown suckers in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; globular bud aloe spreads into colonies by underground suckers rather than surface offsets, so give it room to expand.

directions: Globular bud aloe takes its common name from the tightly rounded, ball-like flower buds packed onto its winter inflorescence, a distinctive shape that opens gradually from dull red buds to ivory-yellow, and finally clear yellow flowers as each raceme matures, a slower and more dramatic color progression than the fairly uniform coral or orange flowers of most southern African aloe species here. Unlike clumping aloes that offset from visible basal pups, it spreads by underground suckers that emerge as new rosettes some distance from the parent plant, gradually forming loose colonies across a bed rather than a tight single clump. Broad, incurved, grayish-green leaves with sharply toothed margins form an evergreen, stemless rosette that stays fairly low to the ground even at maturity. Native to seasonally dry savanna and bushveld from Zimbabwe and Mozambique into northeastern South Africa, it is markedly more frost-tender than highland species like spiral aloe or book aloe and needs a warm, sheltered, frost-free site.

common_name: Erik the Red Aloe (Sunbird Hybrid Aloe)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this large hybrid needs room to develop its eventual six-foot stature and is more frost-tolerant than many of its Madagascan-influenced Kelly Griffin counterparts.

directions: Bred by Leo Thamm of Sunbird Aloes in South Africa from a closely guarded cross reportedly involving Aloe marlothii, A. petricola, A. mawii, and A. arborescens, Erik the Red combines the bulk of a large tree aloe with the intense red-flower display of its arborescens parentage, growing to six feet or more on a single stem topped by a two-foot rosette of long, dark green, softly spined leaves. Its long-lasting spikes of blood-red flowers with contrasting yellow stamens open in early winter and continue blooming for weeks, a notably extended flowering period compared to the shorter bloom windows of species like mountain aloe or Cape aloe. As a complex multi-generation hybrid it is more moderately frost-tolerant than many of its southern African parent species individually, making it a good choice where a large architectural aloe is wanted but hard freezes are an occasional risk. Grow it in full sun with excellent drainage and give it several years to develop its mature, statuesque form.

planting.note: Plant offsets in spring in fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to bright filtered light; Doran Black develops its best rosy-copper stress color under bright light with some drought.

directions: Hybridized by aloe breeder Dick Wright and named for the late nurseryman Doran Black, this cultivar is known as a 'mosaic aloe' for the raised, pale green and white tubercles scattered across its extra-thick, bumpy, dark green leaves, a rough, warty leaf texture distinct from the smooth or lightly spotted foliage of most aloes in this collection. In full sun the leaves whiten and mottle further, shifting toward orange, copper, or rosy-pink under drought or sun stress rather than the reds or bronzes typical of hybrids like Christmas Carol or Van Balen's aloe. It offsets readily around the base to form a dense cluster of rosettes about a foot tall, and produces bell-shaped orange to red flowers on tall spikes that can appear in more than one season. It is comfortable in bright, filtered indoor light as well as outdoor container culture, making it a versatile houseplant-to-patio hybrid.

planting.note: Plant offsets in spring in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix in bright light to full sun; Blizzard is a patented Altman Plants hybrid selected for fast, upright growth and heavy white variegation.

directions: Patented by Altman Plants (US PP21,408), Blizzard was specifically bred to produce a whiter, faster-growing, more upright variegated aloe than its parent lines, and its leaves are almost entirely creamy white with only small irregular flecks of green, a far more extreme variegation than the light speckling seen in Delta Lights or the mottling of Doran Black. The thick, star-shaped rosette holds tiny, soft marginal teeth and stays compact and tidy, making it well suited to a windowsill container rather than an outdoor bed. Clusters of tubular orange to coral-red flowers appear on a tall stalk in late spring through summer, a longer and later bloom window than many winter-flowering aloe hybrids. Because its heavily white leaves have reduced chlorophyll compared to solid-green aloes, give it slightly more consistent bright light to keep it vigorous, and avoid deep shade, which can weaken variegated growth over time.

planting.note: Plant offsets in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to dappled shade; Pink Blush develops its namesake color most strongly with some sun stress and dry soil.

directions: Bred by Kelly Griffin from undisclosed parentage, Pink Blush is grown for its textured, lance-shaped leaves marked with raised pink ridges over a light green to grayish base, a soft rose-toned coloring distinct from the deep red of Cameron's aloe or the coppery orange of golden tooth aloe. Color intensifies from a subtle pink blush toward a stronger rose-pink under bright sun and drought stress, fading toward plain green with shade or extra water. Upright rosettes stay compact and offset moderately to form a small cluster, sending up a short flower stalk of orange blooms from late winter into spring. It suits a xeriscape border, rock garden, or mixed succulent container equally well, and like most Kelly Griffin hybrids benefits from being kept dry and lean rather than fed heavily.

planting.note: Plant offsets in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to mostly shade; Grassy Lassie tolerates more shade than most landscape aloes and is resistant to verticillium wilt.

directions: Marketed as a Proven Winners selection, Grassy Lassie is named for its unusually narrow, grass-like green leaves, a slender, linear leaf shape that stands apart from the broad triangular leaves of most other aloes in this collection, giving established clumps a softer, more textural look reminiscent of an ornamental grass. It tolerates more shade than typical full-sun aloes, growing acceptably from full sun to mostly shaded sites, and is noted for good resistance to verticillium wilt, a soilborne disease that can affect other succulents in humid regions. Orange, tubular flowers appear over an unusually long season spanning fall, winter, spring, and summer rather than a single concentrated bloom period. It is heat tolerant and drought tolerant once established, spreading gradually to form a loose clump about a foot or two tall and wide, useful as a textural accent among bolder-leaved aloes and succulents.
sources: Gardening Gone Wild - Aloes in Kelly Griffin's Garden
